title: The dinosaur at the feeder
question: Why do biologists call birds living dinosaurs?
hook: Every bird you see outside is a dinosaur, and the evidence sits in its family tree.
idea: Birds evolved from earlier theropods, so they are the only living dinosaurs, and crocodilians are their closest living relatives.

beats.prompt: A friend asks which living animals are a bird's closest relatives. What do you tell them?

choices.label: Lizards, because they are the obvious reptile cousin
choices.feedback: Lizards seem the natural pick among reptiles, but they are not the birds' closest living relatives.

choices.label: Mammals, because both groups are warm-blooded
choices.feedback: Warm blood is shared with mammals, but that does not make them close kin to birds.

choices.label: Crocodilians, with which birds form the archosaurs

beats.explain: Birds and crocodilians are each other's closest living relatives and form a clade known as archosaurs.

beats.prompt: Put these events in order, earliest first (the first one is an estimate).
items: Modern birds evolve, about 100 million years ago
An extinction event kills off the pterosaurs and non-ornithuran dinosaurs, 66 million years ago
Willughby and Ray publish the first classification of birds, in 1676
beats.explain: Modern birds evolved about 100 million years ago, the extinction event came 66 million years ago, and the classification work followed in 1676 and 1758.

beats.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The "perching" birds, over half of all species
A group in which flight has been lost
The clade formed by birds and crocodilians
beats.explain: Each term names a part of the bird story, from the science itself to the relatives they share a clade with.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: So birds are the only living dinosaurs.
Their closest living relatives are the crocodilians.
Because birds are warm-blooded, they cannot be reptiles in any modern classification.
beats.explain: In the modern cladistic sense of the term, birds are considered reptiles; their unique morphology and warm-bloodedness are why the older Linnaean system gave them their own class.
